questions.title: Pringles promotion, a motorcycle race, an L-shaped flower bed and an aeroplane cabin layout

subQuestions.questionText:
Gadibolae bought Pringles (chips in a cylindrical container) on promotion at a shop.

**PROMOTION ADVERTISEMENT FOR PRINGLES**

| Detail | Value |
|---|---|
| Promotion offer | 6 Pringles for R100,00 |
| Mass of ONE container | 110 g each |
| Promotion available | From 11 Jan. 2021 to 31 Mar. 2021 |

Determine (in grams) the total mass of the Pringles promotion bought for R100.
subQuestions.memoText:
Total mass:
Mark 1: $6 \times 110\text{ g}$ (1MA multiplying the mass by 6)
Mark 2: $= 660\text{ g}$ (1A mass)
Teaching point: The promotion gives SIX containers, so multiply the mass of one container by six.

subQuestions.questionText:
A single Pringles container is a cylinder with the following dimensions:

| Dimension | Value |
|---|---|
| Diameter | 64 mm |
| Height | 230 mm |

Write down the radius of a single Pringles container.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark 1 & 2: $\text{Radius} = \dfrac{64\text{ mm}}{2} = 32\text{ mm}$ (2A radius)
Teaching point: The radius is always HALF of the diameter.

subQuestions.questionText:
A Pringles container is a cylinder with a diameter of 64 mm and a height of 230 mm.

Choose the letter of the answer that will make the following statement TRUE.

The unit to calculate the inner volume of a Pringles container is …
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark 1 & 2: A (2A correct letter) [accept: mm$^3$]
Teaching point: Volume is a three-dimensional measurement (length $\times$ width $\times$ height), so the unit must be cubed — mm$^3$. Squared units (mm$^2$) are used for AREA.

subQuestions.questionText:
The Pringles promotion is available from 11 January 2021 to 31 March 2021.

NOTE: 2021 was not a leap year, so February had 28 days.

Determine the total number of days this promotion is available.
subQuestions.memoText:
Total number of days from 11 Jan to 31 Mar:
Mark 1: January: $31 - 10 = 21$ days (1MA days in January)
Mark 2: $= (31 - 10) + 28 + 31$ (1MCA adding the days of the 3 months)
Mark 3: $= 21 + 28 + 31 = 80$ days (1CA simplification)
Teaching point: Counting from 11 January means the 1st to the 10th are excluded, so subtract 10 from the 31 days of January. February 2021 had 28 days and March has 31.

subQuestions.questionText:
The promotion advertisement reads: **6 Pringles for R100,00** (each container holds 110 g).

Calculate the price of two 110 g Pringles containers in this promotion.
subQuestions.memoText:
Price for 2 Pringles:
Mark 1: $= 2 \times \left(\dfrac{\text{R}100}{6}\right)$ (1MA dividing the price by 6 and multiplying by 2)
Mark 2: $= 2 \times \text{R}16{,}666\ldots = \text{R}33{,}33$ (1CA simplification) — NPR (no penalty for correct rounding)
Teaching point: First find the unit price of ONE container, then multiply by the number you want.

subQuestions.questionText:
Paul has entered a motorcycle race. A digital clock shows the time he finished the race, and it reads **10:08**.

Two analogue clocks are given:

| Clock | Position of the hands |
|---|---|
| A | The short (hour) hand points just past the 10 and the long (minute) hand points between the 1 and the 2 (about eight minutes past). |
| B | The short (hour) hand points between the 9 and the 10, and the long (minute) hand points just past the 1. |

Choose the item from COLUMN B (A or B) that completes the statement: 'The analogue clock that shows the same time as the digital clock (10:08) is …' Write only the letter.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark 1 & 2: A (2A correct letter)
Teaching point: At 10:08 the hour hand must be just past the 10, and the minute hand must be a little past the 1 (each number on the dial is 5 minutes, so 8 minutes sits between the 1 and the 2).

options.A: The clock whose hour hand is just past 10 and whose minute hand is between the 1 and the 2
options.B: The clock whose hour hand is between 9 and 10 and whose minute hand is just past the 1

subQuestions.questionText:
As Paul's motorcycle crossed the finishing line the instrument on the dashboard showed the following:

| Reading | Value shown |
|---|---|
| Speed needle on the km/h dial | Pointing midway between the 50 and the 70 markings, i.e. on 60 |
| Number window (distance counter) | 680 003 |

Choose the item from COLUMN B that completes the statement: 'Paul's speed is …' Write only the letter (C, D or E).
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark 1 & 2: D (2A correct letter) — accept 60 km/h
Teaching point: The needle on the dial gives the SPEED (km/h). The number window (680 003) is the odometer reading — the total distance the motorcycle has travelled in km, not a speed.

subQuestions.questionText:
A wooden L-shaped flower bed is filled with soil. All corners are right angles. Going around the outside of the bed the printed dimensions are:

| Side | Length |
|---|---|
| Long outer side | 7,3 m |
| Short end | 3 m |
| Missing length | D |
| Long inner side | 5,2 m |
| Short end (other side) | 1 m |

Convert the longest dimension of the L-shaped flower bed to cm.
subQuestions.memoText:
Longest dimension $= 7{,}3\text{ m}$
Mark 1: $7{,}3\text{ m} = 7{,}3 \times 100\text{ cm}$ (1MA multiplying the correct value by 100)
Mark 2: $= 730\text{ cm}$ (1A simplification)
Teaching point: 1 m = 100 cm, so to change metres to centimetres you multiply by 100.

subQuestions.questionText:
The L-shaped flower bed below has all right-angled corners. The dimensions printed on the plan are:

| Side | Length |
|---|---|
| Long outer side | 7,3 m |
| Short end at the top | 3 m |
| Missing length | **D** |
| Long inner side | 5,2 m |
| Short end at the bottom | 1 m |

The missing length D lies opposite the 7,3 m side, in line with the 5,2 m inner side.

Calculate the missing length, **D**.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark 1: $D = 7{,}3\text{ m} - 5{,}2\text{ m}$ (1MA difference of the correct lengths)
Mark 2: $= 2{,}1\text{ m}$ (1CA simplification)
Teaching point: In an L-shape the two lengths on one side must add up to the full length on the opposite side, so the missing piece is the difference between them.

subQuestions.questionText:
The volume of the L-shaped flower bed with materials can be calculated as follows:

Volume = (2,1 m × 3 m × 0,5 m) + (5,2 m × 1 m × 0,5 m)
= 3,15 m³ + 2,6 m³ = 5,75 m³

State which value in the above calculation represents the height of the flower bed.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark 1 & 2: $0{,}5\text{ m}$ (2A height)
Teaching point: Volume of a rectangular box = length $\times$ width $\times$ height. The value that appears in BOTH brackets (0,5 m) is the one dimension the two parts share — the depth/height of the bed.

subQuestions.questionText:
The inside cabin of a small aeroplane is shown on a *layout plan*. All the passenger seats face the front except the seat of the airhostess.

Explain the meaning of a *layout plan*.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark 1 & 2 (2A explanation) — any ONE of:
• A layout plan is a top view that shows the arrangement of features.
OR
• A layout plan is the structural arrangement of items within a certain space.
OR
• A plan of the entire inside cabin, showing the location of seats, exit doors, etc.
OR
• A drawing to scale showing the physical arrangement of all the resources that take up space within a facility.

subQuestions.questionText:
The layout plan of the inside cabin of a small aeroplane shows ten seat columns labelled A (nearest the front) to J (nearest the back) and three rows numbered 1, 2 and 3. The seats present are:

| Row | Seats present |
|---|---|
| 1 | A, B, C, D, E, F, G, H, I, J (10 seats) |
| 2 | B, C, D, E, F, G, H, I, J (9 seats – no seat in column A) |
| 3 | B, C, D, E, F, G, H, I, J (9 seats – no seat in column A) |

The airhostess seat is shown separately at the front, next to the door, and is NOT a passenger seat. The store room and toilet occupy the front-right corner.

Calculate the maximum number of passenger seats available in this aeroplane.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark 1 & 2: $10 + 9 + 9 = 28$ seats (2A number of seats)
Teaching point: Count only the PASSENGER seats — the airhostess seat is not available to passengers.
subQuestions.topic: Maps and plans – Reading a layout plan

subQuestions.questionText:
On the aeroplane layout plan the seat columns are labelled from A (closest to the front) through to J (closest to the back), and the three rows are numbered 1, 2 and 3. All passenger seats face the front.

Stofile is seated in D1. He gets out of his seat and walks past his seat and two more seats towards the back to talk to his friend who is seated on Stofile's right-hand side.

Using the same notation as Stofile's seat, write down the seat number of his friend.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark 1 & 2: **G1** (1A correct seat letter; 1A correct row number)
Teaching point: Moving towards the back from D means passing D, then E, then F — landing on G. The row number stays 1.
subQuestions.topic: Maps and plans – Seating and position

subQuestions.questionText:
During the flight, passengers are allowed to choose a light snack and a drink. The choices are as follows: a muffin or a sandwich, with a cola, a juice or bottled water.

Write down the number of options they can choose from.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark 1 & 2: 6 (2A correct number)
Working: $2\text{ snacks} \times 3\text{ drinks} = 6$ combinations, namely muffin+cola, muffin+juice, muffin+water, sandwich+cola, sandwich+juice, sandwich+water.
Teaching point: When each choice from one list can be paired with every choice from a second list, multiply the number of options in the two lists.

questions.title: Floor plan of Jan's house with a veranda

subQuestions.questionText:
ANNEXURE A shows the floor plan of Jan's house, with a veranda (an open area with a roof over it), in South Africa. The rooms shown on the floor plan are:

| Room | Position on the plan |
|---|---|
| MASTER BEDROOM | top right |
| BATHROOM | small room, upper middle-left |
| KITCHEN | left, middle |
| BEDROOM 2 | centre right |
| DINING | bottom left |
| LIVING | bottom, centre right |
| BEDROOM 1 | bottom left corner |
| VERANDA | bottom right (open, roofed area) |

Write down the number of bedrooms on the floor plan.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark 1 & 2: 3 (2A correct number)
The three bedrooms are the MASTER BEDROOM, BEDROOM 1 and BEDROOM 2.
subQuestions.topic: Maps and plans – Reading a floor plan

subQuestions.questionText:
On the floor plan of Jan's house the veranda is an open roofed area along the bottom-right of the plan. A door leads from the veranda directly into the room that lies immediately above (north of) it on the plan — the LIVING room, which in turn opens on to the passage leading to Bedroom 2, the Master bedroom, the Dining area and the Kitchen.

Which room will be the first room you will enter from the veranda?
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark 1 & 2: The living room (2A correct room)
Teaching point: Follow the door symbol (the quarter-circle arc) from the veranda — it opens straight into the living room.
subQuestions.topic: Maps and plans – Reading a floor plan

subQuestions.questionText:
On ANNEXURE A (the floor plan of Jan's house) a compass arrow marked **N** points diagonally towards the TOP-RIGHT corner of the page. Therefore, on this plan:

| Direction on the page | Compass direction |
|---|---|
| Diagonally up-right | North (N) |
| Diagonally down-right | East (E) |
| Diagonally down-left | South (S) |
| Diagonally up-left | West (W) |

The master bedroom is in the top-right corner of the plan. It has one window (W) on its top wall and one window (W) on its right-hand wall — the wall that faces the top-right/bottom-right corner side of the plan.

In which general direction does the master bedroom window face?
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark 1 & 2: North East (NE) (2A direction)
Teaching point: Use the compass arrow on the plan, not the page. With North pointing diagonally up-right, the master bedroom's right-hand wall faces north-east.

subQuestions.questionText:
The floor plan of Jan's house shows SIX doors in total:

| Door | Type |
|---|---|
| Master bedroom door (off the passage) | Interior |
| Bathroom door | Interior |
| Bedroom 2 door | Interior |
| Bedroom 1 door | Interior |
| Kitchen door leading outside | Exterior |
| Living-room door leading on to the veranda | Exterior |

One of the door locks needs to be changed.

Write down the probability, in simplified fractional form, that it is NOT one of the interior doors.
subQuestions.memoText:
$P(\text{not interior}) = P(\text{exterior})$
Mark 1 & 2: numerator $= 2$ (2RT reading the number of exterior doors)
Mark 3: denominator $= 6$ (1A total number of doors)
Mark 4: $= \dfrac{2}{6} = \dfrac{1}{3}$ (1CA simplification)

OR

Mark 1: $P(\text{not interior}) = 1 - P(\text{interior})$ (1MA probability of NOT)
Mark 2: $= 1 - \dfrac{4}{6}$ (1RT numerator 4)
Mark 3: denominator $= 6$ (1A)
Mark 4: $= \dfrac{2}{6} = \dfrac{1}{3}$ (1CA simplification)
Teaching point: 'NOT interior' is the complement of 'interior', so you may either count the exterior doors directly or subtract the interior-door probability from 1.

subQuestions.questionText:
On the floor plan of Jan's house (in South Africa) the compass arrow **N** points diagonally to the top-right of the page, so the bottom-left side of the plan faces SOUTH and the top-right side faces NORTH.

The kitchen is on the left-hand side of the plan, roughly halfway down, and its window is on the outer left-hand wall — a wall facing towards the south-west/southern side of the house.

Jan remarked that the kitchen gets a lot of sunlight.

Critically comment on his remark.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark 1: Jan is wrong / incorrect (1A opinion)
Marks 2 & 3: The kitchen is on the SOUTHERN side of the house. In South Africa (in the southern hemisphere) the sun is in the northern part of the sky, so a south-facing room does not get a lot of sun. (2O reasoning)
Teaching point: In the southern hemisphere, north-facing rooms get the most sunlight; south-facing rooms are the coolest and darkest.
subQuestions.topic: Maps and plans – Orientation and sunlight

subQuestions.questionText:
An artist's drawing of ONE of the elevations (outside views) of Jan's house shows a single-storey house with a sloping roof, a large window on the left of a front door, a second large window to the right of the door, and a covered veranda running along the right-hand side in front of that second window.

On the floor plan, the kitchen and the dining room are on the OPPOSITE (left/south-western) side of the house; the bathroom window is on the same side as the kitchen, and there is no veranda on that side.

Give ONE reason why the windows shown in the above drawing do NOT represent the windows of the kitchen and the dining room.
subQuestions.memoText:
Marks 1 & 2 (2O reason) — any ONE of:
• It cannot be the view showing the kitchen and dining room, as it does not show the extra window for the bathroom.
OR
• It does not show the other rooms on both sides of the windows.
OR
• It shows the veranda, door, bedroom and living-room windows.
OR
• Because there is no veranda on the side of the kitchen, and the picture shows a veranda.
OR
• The drawing shows the SE elevation while the kitchen is on the SW side.
OR
• The windows shown do not look like kitchen windows — they are too big.
OR
• The drawing represents the front view.
OR
• The kitchen should be on the left-hand side with the window and the door / the door knob is on the right-hand side and not on the left-hand side of the door adjacent to the kitchen window.

subQuestions.questionText:
The scale used for the floor plan of Jan's house is 1 cm representing 1 000 mm in real life.

Write the given scale in number scale format.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark 1: $10\text{ mm} : 1\,000\text{ mm}$ (1A correct ratio with the conversion done)
Mark 2: $= 1 : 100$ (1CA simplification)

OR

Mark 1: $1\text{ cm} : 100\text{ cm}$ (1A correct ratio and conversion)
Mark 2: $= 1 : 100$ (1CA simplification) — AO (answer only gets full marks)
Teaching point: A number scale has NO units, so both sides must first be written in the SAME unit before you simplify.

subQuestions.questionText:
The scale used for the floor plan of Jan's house is 1 cm representing 1 000 mm in real life.

Measuring the inner length of bedroom 2 on the printed floor plan gives **4,4 cm** (any measurement from 4,3 cm to 4,5 cm is accepted).

Use the given scale to calculate the actual length (in m) of bedroom 2.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark 1: Length on floor plan $= 4{,}4\text{ cm}$ (1A correct measurement)
Mark 2: $1\text{ cm} = 100\text{ cm}$, so $4{,}4\text{ cm} = 4{,}4 \times 100\text{ cm}$ (1MCA using the scale)
Mark 3: $= 440\text{ cm}$ (1CA simplification)
Mark 4: $= 4{,}4\text{ m}$ (1C conversion) — accept 4,3 m to 4,5 m

OR

Mark 1: measurement $= 4{,}4\text{ cm}$ (1A)
Mark 2: $1\text{ cm}$ is $1\,000\text{ mm}$, so $4{,}4\text{ cm}$ is $4{,}4 \times 1\,000\text{ mm}$ (1MCA using the scale)
Mark 3: $= 4\,400\text{ mm}$ (1CA simplification)
Mark 4: $4\,400\text{ mm} = 4{,}4\text{ m}$ (1C conversion)
Teaching point: 1 cm on the plan = 1 000 mm = 1 m in real life, so with this scale the measurement in centimetres is simply the real length in metres.
subQuestions.topic: Maps and plans – Working with scale

subQuestions.questionText:
The scale used for the floor plan of Jan's house is a number scale (1 : 100), written as 1 cm representing 1 000 mm in real life.

Jan stated that the given scale is NOT very accurate to use if photocopies were going to be made of the plan.

Critically comment on his statement and give a reason for your answer.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark 1: Jan is correct (1A opinion)
Marks 2 & 3: When a photocopy is made, the size of the plan may change (it may be enlarged or reduced) while the number scale printed on it stays the same, so the stated scale will no longer be true. (2O verification)
Teaching point: A BAR (line) scale enlarges or shrinks together with the drawing, so it stays correct on a photocopy; a NUMBER scale does not.
subQuestions.topic: Maps and plans – Types of scale

questions.title: Tsidi's second-hand bookshelf, painting the backboard and storing files

subQuestions.questionText:
Tsidi needs a bookshelf to store her files. She buys a second-hand wooden bookshelf with two shelves. Its dimensions are:

| Dimension | Value |
|---|---|
| Inside width (length of a shelf) | 162 cm |
| Total outside height | 80 cm |
| Inside height of the bottom shelf | 40 cm |

**A** is the outside length of the bookshelf and **B** is the inside height of the top shelf.

The wood used for the top shelf has a thickness of 1,5 cm all around.

Determine **A**, the outside length of the bookshelf.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark 1: inside length $= 162\text{ cm}$ (1RT reading the inside length)
Mark 2: $A = 162\text{ cm} + 1{,}5\text{ cm} + 1{,}5\text{ cm} = 162\text{ cm} + (1{,}5\text{ cm} \times 2)$ (1MA adding both sides)
Mark 3: $= 165\text{ cm}$ (1CA simplification)
Teaching point: The outside length includes the thickness of the wood on BOTH the left and the right side, so add 1,5 cm twice.

subQuestions.questionText:
Tsidi's bookshelf has the following dimensions:

| Dimension | Value |
|---|---|
| Inside width | 162 cm |
| Total outside height | 80 cm |
| Inside height of the bottom shelf | 40 cm |
| Thickness of the top-shelf wood (all around) | 1,5 cm |
| Thickness of the base of the bottom shelf | 4,5 cm |

Determine **B**, the inside height of the top shelf.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark 1: total height 80 cm and bottom-shelf inside height 40 cm (1RT both heights)
Mark 2: $B = 80\text{ cm} - (40\text{ cm} + 4{,}5\text{ cm} + 1{,}5\text{ cm} + 1{,}5\text{ cm})$ (1MA subtracting)
Mark 3: $= 80\text{ cm} - 47{,}5\text{ cm} = 32{,}5\text{ cm}$ (1CA simplification)
Teaching point: Work from the total outside height and take away everything that is not open space in the top shelf — the bottom-shelf opening (40 cm), the 4,5 cm base, and the 1,5 cm thickness of the shelf below and the top above.

subQuestions.questionText:
The total outside height of Tsidi's bookshelf is 80 cm, which is the same as 31,496 inches.

Determine (rounded to TWO decimal places) the conversion factor for the height in the form **1 inch = … cm**.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark 1: $31{,}496\text{ inches} = 80\text{ cm}$ (1RT height 80 cm)
Mark 2: $1\text{ inch} = \dfrac{80}{31{,}496}\text{ cm}$ (1MA dividing by 31,496)
Mark 3: $= 2{,}54\text{ cm}$ (1A simplification)
Teaching point: To find the value of ONE unit, divide both sides of the statement by the number of units — here divide 80 cm by 31,496 inches.

subQuestions.questionText:
Tsidi bought the bookshelf at a discounted price because the backboard, which covers the entire width and height of the bookshelf, needed painting. She decides to:

• Remove the backboard.
• Paint the back of the backboard with a single coat of paint.
• Paint the front of the backboard with two coats of paint.
• Nail the backboard to the bookshelf.

The outside length of the bookshelf is 165 cm and the total outside height is 80 cm.

NOTE: Area of a rectangle = length × width

Calculate (in cm²) the area of one side of the backboard.
subQuestions.memoText:
Area of a rectangle $=$ length $\times$ width
Mark 1: $= 165\text{ cm} \times 80\text{ cm}$ (1MCA substitution — CA from 3.1.1)
Mark 2: $= 13\,200\text{ cm}^2$ (1CA simplification)
Teaching point: The backboard covers the whole back of the bookshelf, so use the OUTSIDE length and the total outside height.

subQuestions.questionText:
The area of one side of the backboard of Tsidi's bookshelf is 13 200 cm² (it measures 165 cm by 80 cm).

Convert this area to m².
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark 1: $= \dfrac{13\,200}{(100)^2}\text{ m}^2$ (1MCA dividing by $100^2$, i.e. by 10 000)
Mark 2: $= 1{,}32\text{ m}^2$ (1CA simplification)

OR

Area $= 1{,}65\text{ m} \times 0{,}8\text{ m} = 1{,}32\text{ m}^2$ — AO (answer only gets full marks)
Teaching point: $1\text{ m}^2 = 100\text{ cm} \times 100\text{ cm} = 10\,000\text{ cm}^2$, so divide a cm² value by 10 000 to get m².

subQuestions.questionText:
The backboard of Tsidi's bookshelf has an area of 1,32 m² on ONE side. She paints the back of the backboard with a single coat of paint and the front of the backboard with TWO coats of paint (three coats in total).

One litre of paint covers 6,9 m².

Determine (rounded to TWO decimal places) the number of litres of paint required to paint the backboard completely.
subQuestions.memoText:
$1\ \ell$ covers $6{,}9\text{ m}^2$; $n\ \ell$ covers $1{,}32\text{ m}^2$
Mark 1: $n = \dfrac{1{,}32}{6{,}9}$ (1MA dividing by 6,9)
Mark 2: $= 0{,}1913\ldots\ \ell$ (1CA simplification)
Mark 3: For three coats: $0{,}1913\ldots\ \ell \times 3$ (1MA multiplying by 3)
Mark 4: $= 0{,}5739\ldots\ \ell$ (1CA simplification)
Mark 5: $\approx 0{,}57\ \ell$ (1R rounding)

OR

Total area to cover $= 1{,}32\text{ m}^2 \times 3 = 3{,}96\text{ m}^2$ (1MA multiplying by 3; 1CA simplification)
$x = \dfrac{3{,}96}{6{,}9} = 0{,}57\ \ell$ (1MA dividing by 6,9; 1CA simplification; 1R rounding)

OR

Paint needed $= \dfrac{1{,}32 \times 2}{6{,}9} + \dfrac{1{,}32}{6{,}9} = 0{,}38\ \ell + 0{,}19\ \ell = 0{,}57\ \ell$

OR

Spread rate $= \dfrac{1}{6{,}9\text{ m}^2} = 0{,}144\ldots\ \ell/\text{m}^2$; total $= 0{,}144\ldots \times 3{,}96 = 0{,}57\ \ell$
Teaching point: One coat on the back plus two coats on the front means the paint must cover the area THREE times over.

subQuestions.questionText:
Tsidi needs 0,57 ℓ of paint to paint the backboard of her bookshelf completely (one coat on the back and two coats on the front of a board with an area of 1,32 m² per side; 1 ℓ of paint covers 6,9 m²).

Tsidi stated that one 500 mℓ can of paint is sufficient to paint the backboard completely.

Verify, with calculations, whether her statement is valid.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark 1: $0{,}57\ \ell \times 1\,000$ (1MCA — from Q3.3.3, multiply by 1 000)
Mark 2: $= 570\text{ m}\ell$ (1CA simplification)
Mark 3: $570\text{ m}\ell > 500\text{ m}\ell$, so her statement is **NOT valid** (1O verification)

OR

$500\text{ m}\ell \div 1\,000 = 0{,}5\ \ell$, which is less than $0{,}57\ \ell$ — Tsidi's statement is invalid.

OR

$1\ \ell$ covers $6{,}9\text{ m}^2$, so $500\text{ m}\ell$ covers $\dfrac{6{,}9}{2} = 3{,}45\text{ m}^2$; the area to paint is $1{,}32\text{ m}^2 \times 3 = 3{,}96\text{ m}^2$. The paint is not enough — invalid.
Teaching point: Always compare the two amounts in the SAME unit before deciding.

subQuestions.questionText:
Tsidi wants to organise her documents in files. She can store files separately (single files) or in a filing box. The measurements are:

| Item | Measurement |
|---|---|
| Width of a single file | 8,1 cm |
| Width of a filing box | 345 mm |
| Number of single files that fit inside ONE filing box | 4 |

Determine the maximum number of filing boxes that could fit on one shelf, which is 162 cm wide.
subQuestions.memoText:
Number of boxes:
Mark 1: $= \dfrac{162\text{ cm}}{34{,}5\text{ cm}}$ (1MA dividing)
Mark 2: $345\text{ mm} = 34{,}5\text{ cm}$ (1C conversion)
Mark 3: $= 4{,}695\ldots$ (1CA simplification)
Mark 4: $\therefore$ **4 boxes** (1R rounding DOWN)

OR

$= \dfrac{1\,620\text{ mm}}{345\text{ mm}} = 4{,}695\ldots \therefore 4$ boxes (1C conversion; 1MA dividing; 1CA simplification; 1R rounding down)
Teaching point: You cannot fit part of a box on a shelf, so ALWAYS round down when packing whole objects into a fixed space.

subQuestions.questionText:
Tsidi's shelf is 162 cm wide. A single file has a width of 8,1 cm. A filing box is 345 mm wide and holds 4 single files inside it. A maximum of 4 filing boxes fit on the 162 cm shelf.

Calculate the difference in the number of files that she can place on one shelf if she packs the shelf with single files rather than the filing boxes.
subQuestions.memoText:
Number of single files:
Mark 1: $= \dfrac{162\text{ cm}}{8{,}1\text{ cm}}$ (1MA dividing)
Mark 2: $= 20$ files (1A simplification)

Number of files inside the boxes:
Mark 3: $= 4 \text{ boxes} \times 4 \text{ files}$ (1RT number of files in a box)
Mark 4: $= 16$ files (1CA simplification)

Difference:
Mark 5: $= 20 - 16 = 4$ files (1CA difference in files)
Teaching point: The walls of each filing box take up shelf space, so packing files loose fits more of them on the same shelf.

subQuestions.questionText:
Tsidi can store her documents either as single files standing on the shelf, or packed 4 at a time inside filing boxes (a filing box is 345 mm wide and holds 4 single files).

Give a possible reason why Tsidi would prefer the filing boxes.
subQuestions.memoText:
Marks 1 & 2 (2O reason) — any ONE of:
• Neater storage.
OR
• The files stand up straight (they do not fall over).
OR
• It prevents dust from settling on the documents in the files.
OR
• It is easier to separate the files accordingly.
OR
• To categorise / organise her files.
OR
• It prevents the files from breaking or being damaged / it protects the files.

subQuestions.questionText:
Tsidi bought filing boxes to pack the top shelf completely. Four filing boxes fit on the shelf and each filing box holds 4 single files, so there are 16 files on the shelf.

She could not remember in which file she placed a document. She randomly chooses one of the files out of the filing boxes.

Determine, as a percentage to TWO decimal places, the probability that the file she chooses will contain the document she is looking for.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark 1: numerator $= 1$ (1A — only ONE file contains the document)
Mark 2: $P = \dfrac{1}{16} \times 100\%$ (1MCA denominator — CA from 3.4.2)
Mark 3: $= 6{,}25\%$ (1CA simplification)
Teaching point: Probability $=\dfrac{\text{number of favourable outcomes}}{\text{total number of outcomes}}$; multiply by 100 to change it into a percentage.

questions.title: Mr Venter's farmyard layout, a Jojo tank and assembling a chair

subQuestions.questionText:
Mr Venter bought a farm in order to sell chickens and vegetables. ANNEXURE B is the layout plan of the farmyard. The features shown on the plan are:

| Feature | Shape on the plan |
|---|---|
| Livestock barn | Rectangle |
| Chicken site | Circle |
| Vegetable garden | Rectangle |
| Green house | Rectangle |
| Solar greenhouse | Rectangle |
| 80% shade | Rectangle |
| 50% shade | Rectangle |
| Raised seedling beds | Two long narrow rectangles |
| Perennial garden beds | An irregular, many-sided (zig-zag) shape |
| Compost | A small irregular heap next to the green house |
| Garden expansion | Triangle |
| J (three of them) | Jojo tanks (small circles) |

Name the feature on the layout plan which has an irregular shape.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark 1 & 2: Perennial garden bed(s) (2A correct feature)
OR: Compost
Teaching point: An irregular shape is one that is NOT a standard geometric figure (not a rectangle, circle or triangle) — its sides and angles are all different.
subQuestions.topic: Maps and plans – Reading a layout plan

subQuestions.questionText:
On the layout plan of Mr Venter's farmyard the letter **J** appears three times and represents Jojo tanks (water storage tanks).

Give a reason why it is important to have a water tank at one's house.
subQuestions.memoText:
Marks 1 & 2 (2A reason) — any ONE of:
• Water is scarce.
OR
• Rain water is free compared to tap water.
OR
• You pay less on your water bill.
OR
• For water storage.
OR
• To save water for future use.
OR
• To harvest rain water.

subQuestions.questionText:
On Mr Venter's farmyard layout plan the Jojo tanks (marked J) stand next to the green house, the solar greenhouse and the livestock barn. Jojo tanks are usually filled with rainwater.

Write down TWO structures where the water to fill a Jojo tank could possibly come from.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark 1: any ONE correct structure (1A) and Mark 2: a SECOND correct structure (1A) — from:
• The green house roof / its gutters
• The livestock barn roof / its gutters
• The solar greenhouse roof / its gutters
Accept 'roof' and 'gutter/pipe' for full marks (any 2 structures).

subQuestions.questionText:
On Mr Venter's farmyard layout plan the **garden expansion** is a triangle with the following dimensions printed on it:

| Dimension | Value |
|---|---|
| Base (the vertical side) | 17,024 m |
| Perpendicular height (h) | 19,5 m |
| Each of the two slanting sides | 21,28 m |

Calculate (in m²) the area of the garden expansion.

You may use the following formula:

Area of a triangle = ½ × base × height
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark 1: base $= 17{,}024\text{ m}$ (1RT correct base)
Mark 2: height $= 19{,}5\text{ m}$ (1RT correct height)
Mark 3: $\text{Area} = \dfrac{1}{2} \times 17{,}024\text{ m} \times 19{,}5\text{ m} = 165{,}984\text{ m}^2$ (1CA area of a triangle) — NPR
Teaching point: Use the PERPENDICULAR height (19,5 m), not the slanting side (21,28 m).

subQuestions.questionText:
Mr Venter decides to replace the fence around the circular chicken site. The circumference of the circular site is 18,852 m. He is given two cost options for the wire mesh:

| TWO COST OPTIONS FOR THE WIRE MESH | |
|---|---|
| **OPTION A** | R1 154 for a 10 m roll |
| **OPTION B** | R127,30 per running metre |

By means of calculations, advise Mr Venter which option is more economical.
subQuestions.memoText:
**Option A** (rolls of 10 m — he needs 18,852 m, so he must buy 2 whole rolls):
Mark 1: $\text{R}1\,154 \times 2$ (1MA multiplying by 2)
Mark 2: $= \text{R}2\,308$ (1CA Option A cost)

**Option B** (per running metre — 18,852 m rounds up to 19 running metres):
Mark 3: $\text{R}127{,}30 \times 19$ (1MA multiplying by 19)
Mark 4: $= \text{R}2\,418{,}70$ (1CA Option B cost)

Mark 5: **Option A** is more economical, because R2 308 < R2 418,70 (1O best option)
Teaching point: Wire mesh is sold in whole rolls and whole running metres, so round UP in both cases — you cannot buy part of a roll or part of a metre.

subQuestions.questionText:
One of the Jojo tanks on Mr Venter's farm has a 5 000 ℓ capacity. The height of the tank is 220 cm.

NOTE: 1 000 cm³ = 1 ℓ

Calculate (in cm) the radius of the tank.

You may use the following formula:

Volume of a cylindrical tank = 3,142 × (radius)² × height
subQuestions.memoText:
$\text{Volume} = 3{,}142 \times (\text{radius})^2 \times \text{height}$
Mark 1: $5\,000\ \ell = 3{,}142 \times r^2 \times 220\text{ cm}$ (1SF substituting 5 000)
Mark 2: $5\,000\,000\text{ cm}^3 = 691{,}24 \times r^2$ (1C converting $\ell$ to cm³, i.e. $\times 1\,000$)
Mark 3: $r^2 = \dfrac{5\,000\,000}{691{,}24}$ (1M dividing by 691,24)
Mark 4: $r^2 = 7\,233{,}377698$ (1S simplification)
Mark 5: $r = \sqrt{7\,233{,}377698}$ (1M finding the square root)
Mark 6: $r = 85{,}05\text{ cm}$ (1CA radius value) — NPR
Teaching point: The capacity is given in litres but the height in centimetres, so first convert litres to cm³ ($\times 1\,000$) before substituting. Remember to take the SQUARE ROOT at the end, because the formula uses $r^2$.

subQuestions.questionText:
Mr Venter bought a chair which still has to be assembled. The picture of the assembled chair shows these dimensions (in inches):

| Dimension | Value |
|---|---|
| Width of the chair (across the back) | 18" (18 inches) |
| Height of the chair (top of the back to the floor) | 42" |
| Height of the seat above the floor | 22½" |

Write the following as a simplified ratio:

Width of the chair : height of the chair
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark 1: $18 : 42$ (1A correct order and values)
Mark 2: $= 3 : 7$ (1CA simplification — divide both parts by 6)
Teaching point: Keep the parts in the order asked (width first, then height) and divide both by their highest common factor.

subQuestions.questionText:
The height of Mr Venter's chair is 42 inches (42").

Convert the height of the chair to mm.

You may use the following conversions:

1 000 mm = 3,28084 feet    and    12 inches = 1 foot
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark 1: $\text{Height} = \dfrac{42"}{12"} = 3{,}5\text{ feet}$ (1MA converting to feet)
Mark 2: $3{,}28084\text{ feet} = 1\,000\text{ mm}$, so $3{,}5\text{ feet} = \dfrac{3{,}5}{3{,}28084} \times 1\,000$ (1C converting to mm)
Mark 3: $= 1\,066{,}799\ldots\text{ mm} \approx 1\,066{,}8\text{ mm}$ (1CA simplification)

OR

$3{,}28084\text{ feet} = 1\,000\text{ mm}$, so 1 foot $= 304{,}79999\text{ mm}$ (1MA)
12 inches = 304,79999 mm, so $1\text{ inch} = \dfrac{304{,}79999}{12} = 25{,}39999\text{ mm}$ (1C)
$42\text{ inches} = 42 \times 25{,}39999 = 1\,066{,}7999\ldots \approx 1\,066{,}8\text{ mm}$ (1CA) — NPR
Teaching point: Convert in steps — inches to feet, then feet to millimetres.

subQuestions.questionText:
ANNEXURE C shows pictures and written instructions for the first steps to assemble Mr Venter's chair.

**COLUMN A (pictures)**

| Label | What the picture shows |
|---|---|
| (a) | The back frame on its own: two back legs joined by four horizontal back slats, with a short stretcher across the bottom. |
| (b) | An upside-down U-shape: two front legs joined at the top by one stretcher — nothing else attached. |
| (c) | The almost complete chair: front legs and back legs joined by the side stretchers, forming the open seat frame, with the slatted back already in place. |

**COLUMN B (assembly instructions)**

| Label | Instruction |
|---|---|
| (i) | Attach the stretcher to the front legs as shown, using glue and screws. |
| (ii) | Attach the front legs to the back legs with the stretchers. |
| (iii) | Secure the back slats using glue and screws. Position the back stretcher on the legs as shown, then secure using glue and screws. |

Choose an assembly instruction from COLUMN B that matches a picture in COLUMN A. Write only the letter ((i) to (iii)) next to the question numbers 4.3.3(a) to 4.3.3(c).
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark 1: (a) → (iii) (1A correct Roman numeral)
Mark 2: (b) → (i) (1A correct Roman numeral)
Mark 3: (c) → (ii) (1A correct Roman numeral)
Teaching point: Match on what has just been added in each picture — (a) has the back slats and back stretcher fixed, (b) has only the front legs joined by their stretcher, and (c) is the point where the front and back assemblies have been joined by the side stretchers.

subQuestions.questionText:
Two wooden pieces from Mr Venter's chair kit are shown:

| Piece | Description |
|---|---|
| **P** | A short flat bar of even width, square (blunt) at both ends. |
| **Q** | A longer flat bar of even width, square at one end but cut away to a slanted, tapered point at the other end. |

On the assembled chair, the side stretchers run from the front leg back to the slanted back leg, and so one end of each side stretcher has to be cut at an angle to fit against the sloping back leg.

State whether **P** or **Q** represents the side stretcher.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark 1 & 2: **Q** (2A correct letter)
Teaching point: The back legs of the chair slope backwards, so the side stretcher must have one angled (tapered) end to sit flush against them. That is piece Q.
subQuestions.topic: Maps and plans – Interpreting assembly parts

subQuestions.questionText:
On the picture of Mr Venter's assembled chair, four positions on the seat frame are labelled:

| Letter | Position on the chair |
|---|---|
| A | The front-left corner of the seat frame |
| B | The back-left corner of the seat, where the seat meets the left back leg |
| C | The back-right corner of the seat, where the seat meets the right back leg |
| D | The front edge of the seat frame, below the seat |

The seat itself is a square board with TWO notches (small square pieces cut out of the corners along one edge):

| Letter | Position on the seat board |
|---|---|
| S | The notch cut out of the left-hand corner of that edge |
| R | The notch cut out of the right-hand corner of the same edge |

Describe how you would position the seat so that it is attached to the rest of the structure. (Use the given letters A, B, C, D on the picture and S, R on the sketch.)
subQuestions.memoText:
Marks 1 & 2: The seat is placed on top of the side stretchers with the notch labelled **S** placed against **B** (2A mentioning the position of the first notch)
Mark 3: and the notch labelled **R** placed against **C** (1A second notch)
Teaching point: The notches are cut so that the seat can slide around the back legs — so the notched edge must go to the BACK of the chair, S on the left back leg (B) and R on the right back leg (C).

questions.title: Noah the travelling salesman: a road map of the USA, fuel and temperature

subQuestions.label: 5.1.1 (a)
subQuestions.questionText:
Noah is a travelling salesman who lives in the United States of America (USA). He uses a map (ANNEXURE D) to estimate his travelling time between cities. The map shows various cities, the distances (in miles) between cities and the average travelling times (in hours and minutes) between them.

The key reads: 00 = Miles, 0:00 = Time. Example: New York to Lee — distance = 143 miles, time = 3 hours 26 minutes.

The route between Lee and Springfield is marked:

| Route | Distance | Time |
|---|---|---|
| Lee – Springfield | 41 miles | 0:50 |

Choose ONE letter (W, X, Y or Z) that will make the following statement TRUE:

The average time (in hours) to travel between Lee and Springfield is …
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark 1 & 2: **W** (2A correct letter) — accept $\dfrac{50}{60}$
Teaching point: The map gives the time as 0:50, which is 50 MINUTES. To write minutes as a fraction of an hour, divide by 60: $\dfrac{50}{60}$ hours (about 0,83 h). The 41 is the distance in miles, not the time.

subQuestions.label: 5.1.1 (b)
subQuestions.questionText:
On the partial map of the USA (ANNEXURE D) a compass arrow shows that NORTH is towards the top of the map. Relative to Boston, the surrounding cities lie as follows:

| City | Position relative to Boston |
|---|---|
| Providence | To the south-west of Boston |
| Lowell | To the north-west of Boston |
| Gloucester | To the north-east of Boston |
| Plymouth | To the south-east of Boston, down the coast past Brockton |

Choose ONE letter (W, X, Y or Z) that will make the following statement TRUE:

Which city lies southeast of Boston?
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark 1 & 2: **Z** (2A correct letter) — accept Plymouth
Teaching point: South-east means DOWN and to the RIGHT on a map that has north at the top. Plymouth is the only one of the four in that direction from Boston.

subQuestions.label: 5.1.2 (a)
subQuestions.questionText:
The partial map of the USA (ANNEXURE D) gives the distance (in miles) and the average travelling time (in hours and minutes) along each route. Some of the routes shown are:

| Route | Distance (miles) | Time |
|---|---|---|
| Boston – Providence | 52 | 1:05 |
| Boston – Worcester | 44 | 1:00 |
| Boston – Brockton | 25 | 0:35 |
| Springfield – Worcester | 55 | 1:05 |
| Springfield – Lee | 41 | 0:50 |
| Springfield – Hartford | 25 | 0:30 |
| Worcester – Providence | 42 | 0:55 |

Noah found that the same time 01:05 is estimated for travelling from Providence to Boston and from Springfield to Worcester.

Write down the actual distances (in miles) from Providence to Boston and from Springfield to Worcester.
subQuestions.memoText:
Marks 1 & 2: Providence to Boston $= 52$ miles (2RT distance)
Mark 3: Springfield to Worcester $= 55$ miles (1RT distance)
Teaching point: On this map the number WITHOUT a colon is the distance in miles; the number written as h:min is the travelling time.

subQuestions.label: 5.1.2 (b)
subQuestions.questionText:
On the map of the USA, the route from Providence to Boston is 52 miles and takes 01:05, while the route from Springfield to Worcester is 55 miles and also takes 01:05.

Give ONE possible reason why the map indicates the same travelling time for these two different distances.
subQuestions.memoText:
Marks 1 & 2 (2A opinion) — any ONE of:
• The condition or nature of the roads differs.
OR
• The permissible speed / speed limits differ on the two routes.
OR
• The volume of traffic on the road differs.
OR
• The number of traffic lights differs.
OR
• Speed humps / animals / riots / unrest / protest action.
Teaching point: Travelling time depends on the average SPEED you can keep, not only on the distance.

subQuestions.questionText:
Noah travelled from Portland passing three cities (**A**, **B** and **C**) to reach his destination city, **D**.

TABLE 1 below shows the time taken to travel between the various unknown cities indicated by A, B, C and D.

**TABLE 1: TIME TAKEN BETWEEN CITIES**

| START CITY | DESTINATION CITY | TIME TAKEN BETWEEN CITIES |
|---|---|---|
| Portland | A | 01:35 |
| A | B | ½ hour |
| B | C | 00:35 |
| C | D | 1 hour |

The relevant routes on the map (ANNEXURE D) are:

| Route | Distance (miles) | Time |
|---|---|---|
| Portland – Newburyport | 70 | 1:35 |
| Newburyport – Lawrence | 22 | 0:30 |
| Newburyport – Gloucester | 26 | 0:40 |
| Newburyport – Boston | 37 | 0:45 |
| Lawrence – Concord | 41 | 0:50 |
| Lawrence – Lowell | 14 | 0:20 |
| Lawrence – Boston | 29 | 0:35 |
| Lowell – Boston | 28 | 0:40 |
| Lowell – Fitchburg | 33 | 0:40 |
| Boston – Gloucester | 37 | 0:50 |
| Boston – Fitchburg | 46 | 1:10 |
| Boston – Worcester | 44 | 1:00 |
| Boston – Brockton | 25 | 0:35 |
| Boston – Providence | 52 | 1:05 |

Name cities **A**, **B**, **C** and **D**.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark 1: **A = Newburyport** (Portland → Newburyport takes 1:35) (1A)
Mark 2: **B = Lawrence** (Newburyport → Lawrence takes 0:30 = ½ hour) (1A)
Mark 3: **C = Boston** (Lawrence → Boston takes 0:35) (1A)
Mark 4: **D = Worcester** (Boston → Worcester takes 1:00) (1A)
Teaching point: Work through the table one leg at a time, each time looking for the route out of the previous city with exactly that travelling time.

subQuestions.questionText:
The fuel tank of Noah's car has a capacity of 23 gallons. Noah claims that in South Africa it will cost him less than R1 400 to fill up his fuel tank to capacity.

NOTE:
• 1 gallon = 3,785 litres
• Fuel cost R15,97/ℓ  [Source: AA petrol price on 2 March 2021]

Verify, with calculations, whether his claim is valid.
subQuestions.memoText:
Number of litres in 23 gallons:
Mark 1: $= 3{,}785 \times 23$ (1C gallons to litres)
Mark 2: $= 87{,}055\ \ell$ (1S simplification)

Cost of 87,055 litres:
Mark 3: $= 87{,}055 \times \text{R}15{,}97 = \text{R}1\,390{,}27$ (1CA cost of fuel)
Mark 4: R1 390,27 < R1 400, so his claim is **VALID** (1O conclusion)

OR

Number of litres he can buy for R1 400 $= \dfrac{\text{R}1\,400}{\text{R}15{,}97} = 87{,}664\ldots\ \ell$ (1S)
Number of gallons $= \dfrac{87{,}664\ldots}{3{,}785} = 23{,}16$ gallons (1C; 1CA)
He can buy MORE than a full tank with R1 400 — the claim is valid (1O) — NPR
Teaching point: Convert to a common unit (litres) first, then multiply by the price per litre, then compare with R1 400.

subQuestions.questionText:
Noah stays in Greenfield and travels to Fitchburg and back, from Monday to Friday. He fills his car's fuel tank on Monday morning. His tank holds 23 gallons and the fuel consumption of his car is 18 miles per gallon. He refuels his car to capacity as soon as he does not have enough fuel to complete a trip between the two cities.

The route on the map (ANNEXURE D) reads:

| Route | Distance (miles) | Time |
|---|---|---|
| Greenfield – Fitchburg | 49 | 1:05 |

Determine the number of gallons of fuel left in his car's tank on arrival in Greenfield on Friday afternoon.
subQuestions.memoText:
1 full tank $= 23$ gallons.
Mark 1: Distance on a full tank $= 23 \times 18 = 414$ miles (1A travel distance)
Mark 2: Greenfield – Fitchburg $= 49$ miles (1RT trip distance)

Number of one-way trips on 1 full tank:
Mark 3: $= \dfrac{414}{49}$ (1MA dividing)
Mark 4: $= 8{,}448\ldots \therefore 8$ one-way trips on one full tank (1CA number of trips)
Monday to Thursday is $4 \times 2 = 8$ one-way trips $= 392$ miles, so he refills the tank back to 23 gallons after Thursday's return trip.

Fuel used on Friday's return trip ($49 \times 2 = 98$ miles):
Mark 5: $= \dfrac{98}{18}$ (1MA dividing)
Mark 6: $= 5{,}44$ gallons (1CA simplification)

Mark 7: Left in the tank $= 23 - 5{,}44$ (1MA subtracting)
Mark 8: $= 17{,}56$ gallons (1CA simplification)

OR

Single trip $= 49$ miles (1RT); gallons for 1 trip $= 49 \div 18 = 2{,}72$ (1MA, 1A); return trip $= 2{,}72 \times 2 = 5{,}44$ gallons (1CA); $23 \div 5{,}44 = 4{,}22 \approx 4$ days on one tank (1MA, 1CA); left $= 23 - 5{,}44 = 17{,}56$ gallons (1MA, 1CA)

OR

Monday to Thursday: $98 + 98 + 98 + 98 = 392$ miles; he fills up on Thursday. Friday: used $= 98 \div 18 = 5{,}44$ gallons; left $= 23 - 5{,}44 = 17{,}56$ gallons.
Teaching point: A full tank covers $23 \times 18 = 414$ miles, and each day's return trip uses 98 miles. After four days he has used 392 miles' worth — not enough left for Friday's 98 miles — so he refills, and only Friday's trip comes off the new full tank.

subQuestions.questionText:
A temperature reading of –7 °C was displayed on the screen on the dashboard of Noah's car.

Determine (to the nearest ten) the temperature in degrees Fahrenheit.

Use the formula:  °C = ⁵⁄₉ × (°F – 32)
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark 1: $-7 = \dfrac{5}{9} \times (^\circ\text{F} - 32)$ (1SF substitution)
Mark 2: $^\circ\text{F} = \dfrac{9}{5} \times (-7) + 32$ (1S simplification)
Mark 3: $= -12{,}6 + 32 = 19{,}4\ ^\circ\text{F}$ (1CA simplification)
Mark 4: $\approx 20\ ^\circ\text{F}$ (1R rounding to the nearest ten)
Teaching point: Make °F the subject by first multiplying both sides by $\dfrac{9}{5}$ and then adding 32.
